# A further exclusion in the fractional exponential family

Use the proved boundary-stratum reduction in `candidate 9dace055ddbb6578`. Consider a stationary possible minimizer with positive coefficients k copies of 1 and one p, negative coefficients the fixed 1 and m copies of b, where

    0<p,b<1,    k+p=1+mb,    k>=1, m>=k.

The independent signed sum V has density f. Write

    q=phi_+(p)=phi_-(b)<1,
    u=phi_+(1), v=phi_-(1),
    A=phi_+'(p)<0, B=phi_-'(b)<0.

All transforms hold the current f fixed and are those in the reduction note. Convexity of their reciprocals implies u<q and v<q. Euler's identity for the homogeneous probability P gives

    k u+p q-v-mb q=0,

and therefore

    v-q=k(u-q).                                      (1)

Consider the feasible one-dimensional variation increasing p at speed 1 and increasing every negative magnitude b at speed 1/m. All unit coefficients remain fixed. If this point is a local minimum, the second derivative along the variation must be nonnegative.

We compute that derivative and use Euler's identity once more. The general distinct-coefficient Hessian formula is

    P_ij=f(0)[phi(a_i)-phi(a_j)]/(a_i-a_j),

where phi(a)=f_(V+aE')(0)/f(0); for a=-b, phi(a)=phi_-(b). At equal coefficients, the quotient is its derivative. The diagonal is twice that limit. These formulas follow by the same exponential convolution ODE used in the archived positive-coordinate Hessian proof; their signs do not require both coefficients to be positive.

The derivative, along the specified variation, of the first derivative associated with a positive unit is

    f(0)(u-q)(p+b)/[(1-p)(1+b)].

For the negative unit it is

    f(0)(v-q)(p+b)/[(1+p)(1-b)].

For the fractional positive it is 2f(0)A, because all its cross terms with the fractional negatives vanish by stationarity. For each fractional negative coefficient (meaning differentiation with respect to its signed coefficient -b), it is f(0)(m+1)B/m.

Differentiate the Euler identity sum_i a_i P_i=0 along this variation. Its extra term sum_i a_i'P_i vanishes by stationarity. After using (1), the result is

    2pA-b(m+1)B
      = -2k(u-q)(p+b)(p-b)/[(1-p^2)(1-b^2)] =: R.     (2)

The second derivative of P along the variation, divided by f(0), is

    2A-(m+1)B/m
      = (m+1)(k-1)B/(mp)+R/p,                        (3)

where the last equality uses mb=k+p-1.

If p<=b and k>=2, then R<=0 since u-q<0, and the first term in (3) is strictly negative since B<0. Thus this stationary point has a strictly descending second variation and cannot be a local minimum.

If k=1, the balance gives b=p/m. The condition p<=b then forces m=1. In that case the positive and negative random sums both have the law Exp(1)+p Exp(1), independently, and P=1/2 identically.

Consequently a fractional-positive minimizer having probability below 1/2 must satisfy

    p>b, equivalently (m-1)p>k-1.

In particular m>k. This is a strict exclusion of part of the remaining stationary parameter domain. It does not prove the required bound on the remaining domain p>b.
